name: Daria Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you tell me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Daria, 58. My husband Sam and I rent 60 acres at Brook End: 1,200 free-range hens, thirty rare-breed pigs, a few acres of veg and a bit of barley for the pig feed. Three years ago we opened a farm shop in the old dairy, with an egg vending machine at the gate. Our son Leo tests software in the city and our daughter Jas is a vet nurse.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Eggs first, collecting and grading by nine, then the shop opens at ten. Sam does the pigs and the veg. I use AI all day: it writes the Instagram posts, helps me price the sausages, and tells me what to reorder for the shop. I love it when a regular says our eggs taste like her childhood. What wears me out is the £25,000 loan for the shop fit-out and the feed bill, which doubled in five years. There's about three weeks of money in the account, on a good month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So, a bit of a let-down for the tech people. Fine by me, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say on our Instagram that the shop's real anyway, real hens, real people, AI or no AI. In the village I'd say the tools are handy for small businesses and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, nothing changes for us, and that's a mixed bag. The shop's growing slowly, but the loan and the feed bill eat most of it. I'd still be one bad bird flu season away from trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the AI for posts and pricing, because it saves me an hour a day. I'd set aside the vending machine takings each Friday into a separate account, maybe £80 a week. And I'd keep pushing the shop, maybe a Saturday breakfast stall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay. A low hum of worry, mostly about bird flu and the loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened the last time bird flu came close?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two winters ago there was a case eight miles away, and we had to keep the hens inside for four months. Customers stopped paying free-range prices because the eggs technically weren't free-range. We lost about £6,000 that winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If bird flu hit you directly, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cry, then phone the bank. We'd have to sell some pigs early and run the shop on bought-in stock for a while. Sam would go back to driving for the dairy two days a week.

say: I'd post that our shop is **real anyway**: real hens, real people.
I'd tell the village the tools are **handy for small businesses**.
think: The **loan and feed bill** eat most of what the shop earns.
We're still one **bird flu season** away from trouble.
do: Keep using AI for **posts and pricing**, saving an hour a day.
Bank the **vending machine takings**, about £80 a week, every Friday.
Start a **Saturday breakfast** stall at the shop.
feel: Mostly **okay**, with a low hum of worry about **bird flu**.
S0.quote: Customers stopped paying free-range prices because the eggs technically weren't free-range. We lost about £6,000 that winter.
fieldNote: She's a **daily AI user** in the shop side of the business already.
Her risk is **biological and financial**: bird flu, feed costs and a £25,000 loan.
Her backstop is her husband Sam's **dairy driving**, which she names quickly.

steps.text: Keep using AI daily for shop posts and sausage pricing
Bank the vending machine takings, about £80, every Friday
Start a Saturday breakfast stall in the farm shop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing, buying, answering customers. That's my shop side. The hens are still hands-on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say small farms that use these tools well can compete with the big ones for once. I'd put that on our page. At the farmers' market I'd say the same, and offer to show people what I use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it helps me more than it hurts. The AI can do my orders, my answering, my labels, and that frees me for the bit customers pay for, which is me behind the counter. The risk is the supermarkets using the same tools to price eggs to the penny.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd let the AI handle shop ordering and the customer messages, and set up online orders for Friday collection. I'd spend about £1,500 on a proper till system that talks to the AI. And I'd keep an eye on supermarket egg prices every week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, a bit. It's like getting a part-time assistant I can actually afford.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: £1,500 is a lot with three weeks of savings. How would you justify it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If online orders bring in twenty families a week at £15 each, it pays back in five weeks. I've done the sums with the AI, actually, and Sam checked them on paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Sam say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam would say slow down, Daria. Then he'd help me fix the shelving anyway. That's our marriage in two sentences.

say: I'd say small farms can **compete for once** by using these tools well.
I'd offer to **show others** at the farmers' market what I use.
think: AI frees me for **the counter**, which is what customers pay for.
Supermarkets could use the same tools to **price eggs** to the penny.
do: Hand **shop ordering** and customer messages to the AI.
Spend about **£1,500** on a till system linked to online orders.
feel: A bit **excited**, like getting an **affordable assistant**.
S1.quote: Sam would say slow down, Daria. Then he'd help me fix the shelving anyway. That's our marriage in two sentences.
fieldNote: She sees Steady Disruption as **mostly helpful**, since AI takes her desk work, not her hens.
She'd **invest** despite thin savings, backed by a simple payback sum.
The threat she names is **price competition** from supermarkets.

steps.text: Hand shop ordering and customer messages over to AI
Buy a £1,500 till system linked to online Friday orders
Check supermarket egg prices every week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2028, and robots by 2031. I'd be 63, still paying the loan till 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people will want real food from real farms more, not less, when everything else is made by machines. I'd say it on the page and at the market. I'd believe about two thirds of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the thinking AI in 2028 makes my shop work easier. The robots in 2031 are the worry: big egg units with robot collectors could sell eggs at half our price. My only edge is that people like buying from me, and I'm not sure that's enough when money is tight for everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd start farm open days, £8 a head to collect your own eggs and meet the pigs, because a robot can't do that. I'd look at renting a robot weeder for the veg from 2031, rather than buying. We'd cut the barley and buy feed in, which frees Sam for the open days. And I'd clear the shop loan faster with the vending money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but busy-anxious. If I'm doing something, I sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the open days don't work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd go wholesale to the posh restaurants in the city, where Leo knows a few people. Rare-breed pork has a story, and restaurants pay for a story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Leo? His job tests software.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's what keeps me up, actually, more than the hens. My son Leo tests software, and the AI will test software by 2028. He might be coming home to help with the pigs.

say: I'd say people will want **real food** from real farms more, not less.
I'd say it publicly while believing about **two thirds** of it.
think: **Robot egg units** after 2031 could sell eggs at half our price.
My **only edge** is that people like buying from me.
do: Run **farm open days** at £8 a head to collect eggs and meet pigs.
Plan to **rent a robot weeder** for the veg from 2031.
Stop growing **barley** and buy in feed instead.
S2.quote: My son Leo tests software, and the AI will test software by 2028. He might be coming home to help with the pigs.
fieldNote: She splits the dates well: **office AI helps her**, robot egg units threaten her price.
Her plan leans on **experiences** a robot can't sell: open days and stories.
Her deepest worry is her son **Leo's software job**, not her own hens.

steps.text: Run £8-a-head farm open days to collect eggs and meet pigs
Rent a robot weeder for the veg from 2031
Stop growing barley and buy in pig feed
Pay off the shop loan faster with vending money

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, and robots in 2034. The loan's gone by then. That changes it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the best warning small farms could get, so let's use it. I'd run a little evening at the shop for other farm shops on the tools I use. That's how I'd put it out there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I like my chances. The loan's clear in 2030, AGI comes in 2031 and does my office, and by 2034 I could rent robots for the heavy work and keep the shop as the face of it. I'd be 66 and still useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd clear the shop loan first. Then I'd save towards a robot lease from 2033. I'd build the online order list to about 300 families, so the shop's income doesn't depend on passing trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful. A bit tired at the thought of it, but hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Jas?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my daughter Jas to stay a vet nurse, because a frightened dog doesn't want a robot. She'd agree with me for once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that could go wrong for you here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The landlord. If he sees robots making his land worth more, he might want it back to farm himself. We've got eight years left on the tenancy. I'd want to talk to him early.

say: I'd say this is **the best warning** small farms could get.
I'd host an **evening at the shop** teaching other farm shops my tools.
think: The **loan clears** in 2030, before AGI arrives in 2031.
By 2034 I could **rent robots** and keep the shop as the face of it.
do: Build the online order list to **300 families**.
feel: **Hopeful**, if a bit **tired** at the thought.
S3.quote: I'd tell my daughter Jas to stay a vet nurse, because a frightened dog doesn't want a robot.
fieldNote: Five years lets her **clear the loan** before the change, which shifts her mood.
She'd teach other farm shops, a **community role** that fits her style.
A new risk appears: the **landlord** taking the land back to automate.

steps.text: Save towards leasing a robot for the heavy work from 2033
Grow the online order list to 300 families

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Robots by 2039. I'd be 71, and probably still selling eggs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and farm shops like ours could be the winners. I'd say it at the market and online. I'd mean all of it this time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's good for us. The loan's long gone, the AI does the boring half, and by the time robots come I'm 71 and glad of help with the heavy lifting. The money stays thin, but it's thin in a way I know how to handle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep growing the shop steadily, add a café corner in about 2030, and lease a robot for the hen house when they're cheap and proven. I'd keep the AI doing the books. And I'd ask the landlord about a longer tenancy now, while things are calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Properly calm. That doesn't happen often.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the café cost?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe £12,000 for the kitchen bits, which we'd only do once the loan's cleared. I'd want Jas's friend who bakes to run it on a share of the takings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said money stays thin. Does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. Thin money with a growing shop and fewer aches is better than what we've got now. I'd take that deal tomorrow.

say: I'd say ten years is **a gift**, and farm shops could be the winners.
I'd say it **openly** at the market and online.
think: By 2039 I'm 71 and **glad of help** with the heavy lifting.
Money stays **thin**, but in a way I know how to handle.
do: Add a **café corner** for about £12,000 after the loan clears.
Lease a **robot** for the hen house once proven and cheap.
Ask the landlord for a **longer tenancy** now.
feel: **Properly calm**, which she says is rare.
S4.quote: Thin money with a growing shop and fewer aches is better than what we've got now.
fieldNote: With ten years, she sees AI and robots as **good for her business**.
Her calm comes from **planning**, not from having money.
She'd lock in the **tenancy** early, learning from the five-year conversation.

steps.text: Add a £12,000 café corner once the loan is cleared
Lease a robot for the hen house once proven
Ask the landlord for a longer tenancy this year

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Robot egg units would arrive while we're still paying for the shop. What would help is cheap robot leases for small farms, not just sales to big ones, and a bit of protection on our tenancy so landlords can't take the land back to automate it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about customers. Everyone talks about the farmer and the robot. The farm shop survives on whether people still want to buy from a person, and I think they will, if they can afford to.

headlineQuote: The farm shop survives on whether people still want to buy from a person, and I think they will, if they can afford to.
portrait: Daria, 58, rents **60 acres** with her husband Sam, with hens, pigs, veg and a **farm shop**.
She has a **£25,000 shop loan**, about three weeks of savings and constant feed and bird flu worries.
She uses **AI every day** for posts, pricing and ordering, and would lease robots when proven.
She bets on **real people** behind the counter as her edge over robot farms.
She's **anxious** at two years, **uneasy** at five and **calm** at ten.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, when robot egg units would arrive while the shop **loan** is unpaid.
whatWouldHelp: **Tenancy protection** so landlords can't take land back to automate.
